title: The smallest best fit
summary: The point on c + 2m = 3 with the smallest c² + m², and why it is special.

blocks.title: Your open task

define.meaning: Of all the best fits, the one nearest the origin: the smallest $\|p\|^2 = c^2 + m^2$.

blocks.why: With a whole line of equally good fits, 'smallest' is the natural tie-break, and it is the one the pseudo-inverse returns.
blocks.prompt: This is where you stopped: find the point on $c + 2m = 3$ with the smallest $c^2 + m^2$. First write $c$ in terms of $m$.

slips.say: Moving $2m$ to the other side flips its sign.
That is $-(3 - 2m)$. Check which side the 3 ends up on.

hints: Get $c$ on its own on one side.
Take $2m$ away from both sides of $c + 2m = 3$.

blocks.title: One variable
blocks.why: With $c$ replaced, $c^2 + m^2$ becomes a parabola in $m$, and parabolas are easy to minimise.
blocks.prompt: Put $c = 3 - 2m$ into $c^2 + m^2$ and expand. Type it as a polynomial in $m$, like `am^2 + bm + k`.

slips.say: $(3 - 2m)^2$ has a middle term: $(3 - 2m)(3 - 2m)$ gives $3 \cdot (-2m)$ and $(-2m) \cdot 3$.
The middle term comes twice: $3 \cdot (-2m)$ and $(-2m) \cdot 3$.
That is $c^2$ alone. Don't forget the $+\,m^2$.

check.say: Put $m = 0$ into your polynomial: you should get 9, which is $c^2 + m^2$ at $(3, 0)$. At $m = 1$ you should get 2, for the point $(1, 1)$.

blocks.title: The bottom of the parabola
blocks.why: A parabola that opens upwards is smallest where its slope is zero.
hints: Differentiate with respect to $m$ and set the result to zero.

blocks.title: And c
blocks.why: The point itself, not just one coordinate.

slips.say: In $c = 3 - 2m$ the $2m$ is taken away, not added.

blocks.solution: So $p = (0.6, 1.2)$: the answer to the task you were set.
blocks.next: How far is it from the origin?

blocks.title: How small?
blocks.why: Comparing it with other best fits shows it really is the smallest.

check.say: Slide $p$ along the line: the circle through $p$ shrinks until it just touches the line. Or put $m = 1.2$ into $5m^2 - 12m + 9$.

blocks.solution: Smaller than any other best fit: $(1, 1)$ gives 2 and $(3, 0)$ gives 9.

blocks.title: The direction A can't see

define.meaning: The vectors $d$ with $Ad = 0$. Adding one to a best fit changes nothing $A$ can see.

blocks.why: Moving along the line of best fits is adding multiples of one null-space direction. That direction explains which point is smallest.
blocks.prompt: Find a non-zero $d = (d_1, d_2)$ with $Ad = 0$. Any multiple will do.

answer.acceptNote: Any non-zero multiple of $(2, -1)$ is the same direction.

hints: Each row of $Ad$ is $d_1 + 2d_2$; you need that to be 0.
Pick $d_2 = -1$ (or any non-zero number) and solve for $d_1$.

blocks.title: p and the null space
blocks.why: This is the property the pseudo-inverse is built to have.
hints: Multiply entry by entry and add.
blocks.solution: The smallest best fit has no part along the null space. Every best fit is $p + t\,d$, and because $p \perp d$, $\|p + t\,d\|^2 = \|p\|^2 + t^2\|d\|^2$, smallest at $t = 0$. The pseudo-inverse builds this in: that is the next lesson.
